title: 6 Insane Documentary Editing Techniques in CapCut
one_sentence_summary: Learn six high-level CapCut editing techniques—such as focus shifting, glass texture screen recording, film framing, and parallax depth—to transform simple videos into cinematic, Vox-style documentary edits.
key_takeaways: Create dynamic focus-shift effects by separating elements into compound layers, keyframing position and blur transitions, and applying speed-easing curves.
Make boring on-screen research compelling by overlaying scanned documents using the 'Multiply' blend mode, speeding up playback, and adding audio risers.
Elevate text design by selecting professional documentary fonts like Special Elite, Tafel Sans Pro, or Helvetica Black Condensed, and setting text animation duration between 1.5 to 2 seconds.
Age modern footage into authentic historical archives using the 'Film Frame 2' filter combined with lowered saturation, elevated contrast, and added particle/fade effects.
Give raw screen recordings a realistic monitor-lens look by adding an RGB glass texture overlay (such as TextureLabs Glass 127) using 'Color Burn' blend mode at roughly 39% opacity.
Build a 3D parallax feel by copying location/scale attributes between background and foreground compound clips while slightly offsetting scale and position keyframes.

actionable_frameworks.name: Screen Recording Texture Overlay Method
actionable_frameworks.description: Place an RGB pixel/glass texture image over a screen recording in CapCut, set the blend mode to 'Color Burn' (or similar), and lower opacity to around 30-40% to mimic footage shot off a physical monitor.

actionable_frameworks.name: Rack Focus Layering Workflow
actionable_frameworks.description: Isolate foreground and background subjects using background removal and rectangle masks with ~20px feathering, compound the clips, and keyframe opposite blur values (0 to 50 and 50 to 0) along with eazed motion curves.

memorable_quotes: You can craft the most incredible edit, the most incredible video in the world, but if you get this wrong, you'll still look like an amateur.
